title: Imagine the scene
hook: Ignatius asks you to enter a gospel story with all your senses

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first week: honest sorrow, held by mercy. Your line was loved, as I am. Did you let one regret sit inside that mercy, even for a moment? Day one thousand one hundred forty-two.

Dust on the road out of Jericho. A crowd moving, loud, pushing. At the edge of the road sits a blind beggar named Bartimaeus. He hears that Jesus of Nazareth is passing, and he starts shouting. People tell him to be quiet. He shouts louder. Jesus stops. Mark's Gospel tells it in a handful of lines. Ignatius of Loyola, whose Spiritual Exercises we've been walking through, would slow it right down. He'd ask you to stand on that road. Feel the grit. Hear the crowd. Watch the beggar throw off his cloak and jump up. Today's practice has a plain name, and the name is the instruction: imagine the scene.
screen: `A BLIND MAN ON THE JERICHO ROAD.`
`THE CROWD SAYS HUSH. HE SHOUTS LOUDER.`

segments.voice: In the Exercises, Ignatius opens many prayer times with what he calls a composition of place: seeing the spot where the story happens. For the birth of Jesus, he suggests picturing the road from Nazareth to Bethlehem, how long it is, how wide, whether it runs flat or through valleys. He isn't after a history lesson. He's after presence. Then he goes further. Later in the day, he suggests going back over the same scene one sense at a time: what you'd see, what you'd hear, even what you'd smell and taste and touch. This second move is known as the application of the senses. Why bother? Because a story read from a distance stays on the page. A story you stand inside starts asking you things. On the Jericho road, Jesus asks Bartimaeus a strange question. Anyone can see what the man needs. Still Jesus says, in the King James words: "What wilt thou that I should do unto thee?" And Bartimaeus answers: "Lord, that I might receive my sight." From a distance, that's an exchange between two men long ago. Standing on the road, the question can turn and land on the one praying. What do you want? Ignatius trusted that God could work through the imagination, and he didn't treat it as making things up. The details someone supplies may not match the real road, and that's all right. The gospel text stays the anchor; the imagined scene is a way of paying close attention to it. For some, pictures come easily. Others see almost nothing and mostly hear, or only sense the mood. Some teachers of this prayer say one sense is enough to begin.
screen: `WHAT WILT THOU THAT I SHOULD DO UNTO THEE?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: imagine one gospel scene. Choose the Jericho road, or any story you know. Close your eyes if you like. First, the place: the ground under your feet, the light, how far off Jesus is. Then go sense by sense: the crowd's noise, the dust, the warmth of the day. Find where you're standing. Maybe you're in the crowd. Maybe you're the one by the road. Let the question reach you: what do you want? If you pray, you can answer him. If not, just notice what answer comes. The bell holds the time.
Imagine the scene. Ignatius' way into a gospel story: see the place, use each sense, and let the story speak back.
Your line: step into the story. Today, take one ordinary moment, a kitchen, a bus, a line at the store, and take it in with every sense before you move on. Day one thousand one hundred forty-two.

screen: `DAY 1142 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE CALL OF THE KING.`

howItsDone: In Ignatian prayer, people often read a short gospel passage, picture the place, enter the scene with their senses, and then speak with Jesus about what stirred; retreat guides and spiritual directors often lead this.

fork.setup: you're Bartimaeus by the road. Jesus is passing, and the crowd tells you to be quiet. what do you do?
options: go quiet and hope for another day.
ask someone in the crowd to pass on a message.
fork.reveal: in Mark he cries out all the more. Jesus stops, calls for him, and asks what he wants.

what a scholar hears: the Exercises name two moves here: a composition of place, and later an application of the senses.

notes: Paraphrases Ignatius: the composition of place, the Nativity contemplation's road from Nazareth to Bethlehem (length, breadth, level or through valleys), and the application of the senses later in the day. Confirm wording and placement in the Second Week.
'Ignatius trusted that God could work through the imagination' is a general description of Ignatian prayer; confirm or soften.
Dust, grit and heat in the hook and practice are imaginative details in the spirit of the exercise, not in Mark's text; the cloak is Mark 10:50.
Fork reveal paraphrases Mark 10:48–49 ('he cried the more a great deal').
Index word 'Imagine the scene' is a title head; the hook avoids opening with 'Imagine' per the house rule.

Editor: cut the overstatement that Ignatius 'would not let you read it in a handful of lines'; 'teachers of this way call it' changed to 'this second move is known as' (the name is the Exercises' own); 'teachers say one sense is enough' softened to 'some teachers' in teach and myth.
